messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] MCDS : What's the right way of dealing with "no observation" data ?
messages.body_plain:
Hypolais

It sounds as if your data organisation to prepare data for import into Distance is quite complex.  I take from your description you are preparing a Distance project for each species.  It might be easier to create a multi-species Distance project, then use the data filtering capability inside Distance to produce species-specific estimates.  A side-benefit of creating a multi-species project is (perhaps) fewer stations without detections of any species.

I raise this organisation possibility because there is an example of this provided as a sample project provided with Distance (songbird).  The data and analysis is described in Buckland et al. (2001) Section 8.7 as well as in Knopf et al. 1988 JWM 52:280-290.  That study was a 2-year study (like yours) with multiple replicate area (pastures).  The year and pastures constituted strata in the data structure.  Using the Distance software, these authors produce year-specific density estimates.

Have a look at this project and see if it will suit your study objective.  If so, it may make your data preparation easier and make your analysis straightforward.

messages.subject_clean: point-transect hybrids or transects with rounded ends
messages.body_plain:
I am not sure how to search for this topic, so please point me in the right direction if this issue has already been addressed.

I am interested in applying distance sampling to data from nest searches along transects. Surveyors initially record detections of individuals (white-headed woodpeckers) along the transect, and then followed detected individuals back to their nests. We then recorded spatial coordinates for nest locations, for which frequency declines with distance to the transect. I want to estimate nest density and model nest density as a function of habitat.

When searching for nests, surveyors are not restricted to areas perpendicular to the transect, so some nests were located off the ends of transects. Thus, sampling units are actually something of a hybrid between points and transects (rounded at the ends, rectangular along the body).

I am wondering if anyone has looked into or thought about how to model detection probability in this scenario, and specifically how to get (g[d]) from density (f[d], where r is the distance to the object subject to detection). Given that for line transects f(d) = g(d), and for points f(d) = d*g(d), I imagine that for rounded-end transects the conversion equation is somewhere in between these. For example, we could model f(d) = A*d*g(d), where 0 < A < 1, and A = f(L * ESW), where L is the length of the transect and ESW is effective strip width, which would depend on detection probability. So, for very short transects A ~= 0 and the the situation would approach that of a survey point, for very long transects A ~= 1 and the situation would approach that of a line transect, and with A ~= 0.5 (i.e., the hybrid situation) the conversion factor between f(d) and g(d) would depend on detection probability.

Has anyone attempted to develop this or a comparable approach for rounded-end transects? If not, would you have any suggestions for developing this idea further?

Also, on a tangential note, another issue I have to deal with is that some of my rounded-end transects bend, so I'd appreciate any suggestions for references that describe how to deal with non-linear transects. I have found a couple references so far:

Hiby, L., and M. B. Krishna. 2001. Line transect sampling from a curving path. Biometrics 57:727-731.

Strindberg, S., and S. T. Buckland. 2004. Zigzag survey designs in line transect sampling. Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics 9:443.

I'd appreciate any suggestions for more recent references that preferably provide a generalized framework for dealing with curvy or bendy transects.

Thanks in advance!

Quresh

messages.body_plain:
Ana

I think you would first want to establish whether the influence of your vegetation covariate is very strong.  You can establish that by setting a filter to exclude observations without the covariate; fit models with and without the covariate to determine if the covariate is meaningful.  Recognise also, in contrast to mark-recapture estimation, distance sampling is robust to unmodelled heterogeneity (called pooling robustness--see Section 11.12 of Advanced Distance Sampling by Buckland et al. (2004).

If you have established that you wish to conduct the hybrid analysis you describe in your question, then you could consider using the mark-recapture distance sampling engine (MRDS) for your analysis; described in Chapter 10 of the Distance 7.1 users guide.  In that chapter there is a description of how to organise your data as well as a section entitled "Using a previously fitted detection function to estimate density in MRDS".  This section addresses you situation.

Hi there, my name is Kevin Hawkshaw and I'm a PhD student at the University of Alberta. I'm working with a dsm modeling abundance for various avian and mammalian groups in an arctic system. I have a bit of an conundrum when it comes to deciding on a response family based on the diagnostic plots of gam.check. I've tried quasipoisson, Tweedie and negative binomial.

the qq plot for the quasipoisson distribution looks pretty bad, so i more or less ruled that one out.
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Z6EJ9CNDkR8/WdqVAT3zkrI/AAAAAAAAANg/ok8DEcdZEokcS4oJufXntCvqOdiW9HrlwCLcBGAs/s1600/mod14_qp_gc.jpeg>
Tweedie response is quite good for the majority of the distribution on the qq plot, however there is evidence of overdispersion at the upper end of the distribution driven by maybe a dozen abnormally large segment counts, and these are not sampling errors.
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-HvGIxIYxcHw/WdqVL5ncz5I/AAAAAAAAANk/lJVpYLzKpXAhiBoeojLUNL3MEa9HtKPygCLcBGAs/s1600/mod14_tw_gc.jpeg>
I then tried the negative binomial distribution, which does much better with the overdispersion, but develops this weird kink at the lower end of the distribution, which (if i have this right) is evidence of some unmodeled zero inflation.
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-1-3HU333fEA/WdqVXjIe5uI/AAAAAAAAANo/yMF9AsdnMCU-CL72FOzr2532MKhXawyhwCLcBGAs/s1600/mod14_nb_gc.jpeg>
i'm also concerned by the unusual looking histogram of residuals which looks more bimodal than normal. my dataset is decent sized (>1000 observations, >2000 segments), so there shouldn't be sample size issues. Can anyone offer some advice here? what is the lesser of these three evils? is there another response family that might fit my data better? happy to provide more information if I haven't done a good job explaining.

Thanks very much,
Kevin

Hi Sara,

The questions you ask are perhaps too much about details - how to implement a design in Distance, when, from your wording, you seem to have trouble with GIS and shapefiles. First you need to think about the big picture.

The most important thing is that you should make sure that your transects are perpendicular to any density gradients that you might expect, so that the usual assumption about sensors being located at random with respect to objects is respected (conversely, if you put transects going along the beach it will, almost for sure, be violated). In a beach, I would say that means that you would ideally have transects perpendicular to the shore line.

I would simply have my transects systematically spaced x meters apart with a random start, with the actual spacing dependent on the available effort.

If the beach is quite wide and long it might be more efficient to have a zig-zag design.

Hope this helps,

T

messages.subject: Left truncation and ESW
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am analysing acoustically-derived slant ranges to sperm whales, as proxies for perpendicular distances to animals from transect lines.  My data-set has a distinct lack of ranges within about 900 m of the trackline.  The histogram of the slant ranges resembles the effect of responsive movement away from the survey vessel, but I don't think this is what has happened - sperm whales are quite robust to the everyday presence of shipping.  The slant ranges overestimate the true perpendicular distances to surface positions above whales foraging at depth.  Many whales probably only become available for acoustic detection when they dive and begin echolocating at 200-400 m depth, so i think it is unlikely that slant ranges would be represented in bins close to the trackline.

If this is the case - a measurement issue rather than an effect of responsive movement - how best should i deal with it when estimating sperm whale density?

I have experimented with left truncating the data at 1000 m, and this gives a very good fit for the detection function.  I notice however, that the ESW then becomes much smaller (from 3600 m to ~2500 m).  My question is, should I add the truncation distance to the ESW to account for the distance surveyed from the trackline?

Another approach I've looked at is grouping the data and using an asymmetrically large first bin, from e.g. 0-2000 m.  The model does not fit as well like this, but is it a better approach?  This way the data from close to the track are not discarded.

As it is more likely that whales detected acoustically are at depths beyond 200 m rather than at the surface, is it valid to adjust the slant ranges by assuming the whales' depths to be e.g. 300 m?  A modelled adjustment considering variation in diving behaviour is beyond me at this point, but simply changing the reference depth to 300 m (via Pythagoras) would seem more realistic than assuming 0 m for this species.

Please excuse my rambling email, I'd appreciate your feedback - thanks,

Chris

Chris

If, as you say, this is a rare event, I would suggest the second course of action you propose: ignore the detection--distance sampling permits failure to detect animals.  The detection contains no information helpful in the fitting of a detection function.

In more extreme situations, there is some discussion in Chapter 8 (CDS) of the users guide for an approach in which detections with missing distances can be included in estimation of encounter rate (and encounter rate variance):

Missing Data in CDS Analysis
Missing Distances
The conventional distance sampling engine is not designed to deal explicitly with missing distance data.  With good field methods, it should be very rare that
you detected an object but did not record a distance for it.  However, if this does occur you have two options:
• Discard the observations with missing distances and analyze the  data as usual.  So long as the observations were not at zero distance, this should cause no bias, as you are effectively just making the detection function steeper by discarding some observations that were made away from the line or point.  A disadvantage of this approach is that you are discarding data that could help to estimate encounter rate, so the overall variance may be higher than the second approach.
• Use a data filter to select only the observations with recorded distances.  Fit a detection function to these data, and record the estimated probability of detection and SE.  Enter these as multiplers and the estimate density/abundance using the whole dataset, as described under Multipliers in CDS Analysis.  Note an important assumption here is that the missing distances are missing at random – for example it will not work if you are less likely to record the distance for objects farther from the line or point.  For this reason, the first approach is probably safer.  Note also that this approach won’t work if you use stratification – in that case you’ll
need more than one multiplier (one for each stratum), and will have to calculate the global density estimate by hand.

messages.body_plain:
Bhaskar

Strictly speaking, line transect sampling does not specify what time of day sampling should be performed.  This is a matter related to the biology of your study animal.  If the bird is readily seen/heard at one time of day, then that is the most efficient time of day to sample.

Likewise, distance sampling does not formulate the question of sampling effort in terms of proportion of study area to cover.   Rather, sampling effort is considered in terms of the number of replicate transects and number of animal detections.  When developing your sampling design, strive to have a reasonable number of transects (~20), placed in a systematically random manner, not following roads or tracks to provide spatial replication across your study area.  Furthermore, strive to produce ~60 detections of your study animal so you can do a credible job of estimating a detection function.

You can gain a sense of the total length of transects needed to produce your 60 detections if you have conducted a small pilot survey, noting the number of detections you make over a known length of transects. messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris, list,

First, your question about left truncation: if you have run the analysis in Distance and selected left truncation in the Truncation tab, then there is nothing else that you need to do – the calculations will take account of the truncation.  There is more information about left truncation in the Distance help file.

It is true that an advantage of binning data is that you don’t discard data – but actually, in this case, neither left truncation nor binning at closer ranges will solve the problem of measuring direct (slant) ranges to animals at unknown depth, rather than perpendicular ranges.  This is because the issue of slant ranges affects all observations, not just those that were close to the transect line.  Therefore, your third suggestion of correcting all distances by making some assumption of animal depth is the best option of the three approaches.

There is a paper by Barlow and Taylor (2005) that explored doing the same for another sperm whale dataset.

Barlow, J. & Taylor, B. 2005. Estimates of sperm whale abundance in the northeastern temperate Pacific from a combined acoustic and visual survey. Marine Mammal Science 21, 429-445.

I hope some of this helps.

Thanks,

Danielle

Sent: 11 October 2017 22:07
To: distance-sampling
Subject: [distance-sampling] Left truncation and ESW

Hello,

I am analysing acoustically-derived slant ranges to sperm whales, as proxies for perpendicular distances to animals from transect lines.  My data-set has a distinct lack of ranges within about 900 m of the trackline.  The histogram of the slant ranges resembles the effect of responsive movement away from the survey vessel, but I don't think this is what has happened - sperm whales are quite robust to the everyday presence of shipping.  The slant ranges overestimate the true perpendicular distances to surface positions above whales foraging at depth.  Many whales probably only become available for acoustic detection when they dive and begin echolocating at 200-400 m depth, so i think it is unlikely that slant ranges would be represented in bins close to the trackline.

If this is the case - a measurement issue rather than an effect of responsive movement - how best should i deal with it when estimating sperm whale density?

I have experimented with left truncating the data at 1000 m, and this gives a very good fit for the detection function.  I notice however, that the ESW then becomes much smaller (from 3600 m to ~2500 m).  My question is, should I add the truncation distance to the ESW to account for the distance surveyed from the trackline?

Another approach I've looked at is grouping the data and using an asymmetrically large first bin, from e.g. 0-2000 m.  The model does not fit as well like this, but is it a better approach?  This way the data from close to the track are not discarded.

As it is more likely that whales detected acoustically are at depths beyond 200 m rather than at the surface, is it valid to adjust the slant ranges by assuming the whales' depths to be e.g. 300 m?  A modelled adjustment considering variation in diving behaviour is beyond me at this point, but simply changing the reference depth to 300 m (via Pythagoras) would seem more realistic than assuming 0 m for this species.

Please excuse my rambling email, I'd appreciate your feedback - thanks,

Chris

messages.subject: Stratified Sampling Design
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

For my thesis I'm helping with my state wildlife agency's (Texas) redesign of their annual survey for white-winged dove. The ecology of the species has shifted and white-wings now occupy (almost) exclusively urban areas across the entire state as opposed to open woodlands in South Texas. They will venture outside of cities during the day, but for nesting and roosting, they stay within urban areas. As such, the state designed their original survey in 2008 using a stratified design that targets the larger cities. The point placement process used a 500m grid with points at each intersection, points greater than 100m from a public road were removed and those remaining were snapped to the nearest road (and yes I know this biases estimates but biologists can't go traipsing through homeowner's backyards). Each year, a selection of cities (usually around 200) are sampled once via point counts. The number of points varies between cities depending on the size but the lowest number of points is 10 and the largest is 180. In any given year, there are 266 cities that can be surveyed; 156 have 15 points and 43 have 30 just to give you an idea of the scope of the survey.

After 9 years of the survey, the state has decided they want to take more of a classical sampling approach by which they focus more effort on areas with higher abundance to increase the efficiency of the survey. I am now tasked with determining how many/which cities need to be surveyed and how many points each one of those cities must have to keep the variance on the statewide population estimate at an acceptable level. The focus is on statewide and regional abundances; the state isn't overly concerned with dove abundances at the city level (the regional level refers to a subpopulation analysis we did previously; there's 5 across the state of Texas). That being said, I have stratified my densities by each city so that I can attempt to extrapolate them to non-surveyed cities using covariates from a hierarchical model (another topic entirely). This is a necessary process as cities that are not surveyed account for approximately 18,100 of 43,500 square kilometers of potential dove habitat. Just using a rough population estimate from a CDS analysis and assuming densities of non-surveyed cities were the same as the average regional densities, these non-surveyed areas can inflate state abundance estimates by 5 million birds.

 So, onto the actual question... I apologize for the long setup. What is the best way to go about adjusting the number of points for a given city based on its density/abundance? I'm assuming that adjusting the number of points by city is the way to go since 1) white-winged dove do not occupy the space between cities and 2) obtaining density estimates by city is a necessary process so that we can extrapolate to non-surveyed areas using covariates.

 I know I could use the equation from 7.2.2.2 of the Introduction to Distance Sampling text to correct the number of points but I've run into some issues with some example calculations. In the following examples, I want to lower the CV to 0.2 and I assume b = 3:

Burnet, TX Estimates for 2016

cv_density=40.45; k_0= 14; n_0 = 10

k=(3/{0.2}^2)*(14/10)
k=105 points needed

but if the CV is already less than 0.2:

Winters, TX estimates for 2016

cv_density=17.61; k_0 = 15; n_0 = 35
k=32.14 points needed

Shouldn't the number of necessary points be lower since we have some room to spare?

In the Advanced Distance Sampling text, Section 7.2.1.4 references the Underwood (2004) dissertation which sounds like what I am trying to do (allocate points with probability proportional to expected density), however, I cannot find it online.

Another option that I suppose is possible but not necessarily "good" would be to calculate the number of points needed at the state or regional level to bring the CV to XX% and then allocating points (using the same placement system as the original survey) to the cities with largest abundances until we run out of points.

Does anyone have any recommendations?

Thanks in advance,

Conor McInnerney

Hi Kevin, hi listfolk,

The squareness of the segments is by no means essential for the DSM approach to work. Things to bear in mind are:

- not having segments to short that you end up "binarising" your response (i.e., just 1s and 0s)
- not making segments so long that there is little information about spatial pattern
- enabling use of any spatial predictors at the resolution that would be meaningful (e.g., not averaging over SST such that there's so information to build a model)

Hope this helps!

cheers,

> Hello,

The ecology of the species has shifted and white-wings now occupy (almost) exclusively urban areas across the entire state as opposed to open woodlands in South Texas. They will venture outside of cities during the day, but for nesting and roosting, they stay within urban areas. As such, the state designed their original survey in 2008 using a stratified design that targets the larger cities. The point placement process used a 500m grid with points at each intersection, points greater than 100m from a public road were removed and those remaining were snapped to the nearest road (and yes I know this biases estimates but biologists can't go traipsing through homeowner's backyards). Each year, a selection of cities (usually around 200) are sampled once via point counts. The number of points varies between cities depending on the size but the lowest number of points is 10 and the largest is 180. In any given year, there are 266 cities that can be surveyed; 156 have 15 points and 43 have 30 just to give you an idea of the scope of the survey.
>
> After 9 years of the survey, the state has decided they want to take more of a classical sampling approach by which they focus more effort on areas with higher abundance to increase the efficiency of the survey. I am now tasked with determining how many/which cities need to be surveyed and how many points each one of those cities must have to keep the variance on the statewide population estimate at an acceptable level. The focus is on statewide and regional abundances; the state isn't overly concerned with dove abundances at the city level (the regional level refers to a subpopulation analysis we did previously; there's 5 across the state of Texas). That being said, I have stratified my densities by each city so that I can attempt to extrapolate them to non-surveyed cities using covariates from a hierarchical model (another topic entirely). This is a necessary process as cities that are not surveyed account for approximately 18,100 of 43,500 square kilometers of potential dove habitat. Just using a rough population estimate from a CDS analysis and assuming densities of non-surveyed cities were the same as the average regional densities, these non-surveyed areas can inflate state abundance estimates by 5 million birds.
>

messages.subject_clean: Allocating effort in systematic parallel design .... bug?
messages.body_plain:
Hi

We are planning a small pelagic fish transect survey using a systematic parallel design. Generating random parallel designs seems to work fine but when we try to generate a systematic design the effort units seem to be mixed up. The study area (Bangladesh continental shelf) is wider than high so about 6 lines at angle 0 use up our available 1700 n.mi. of transect. However, because of the shelf slope we want to run the survey at an angle of 75 degrees but the allocation of 6 lines seems to be permanently fixed and neither the real-time effort update or the manual effort update seems to affect it. As a result, at 75 degrees we get very widely separated lines and in fact only 1 or 2 even show up, not even 6. At 75 degrees there should be 24-26 transects rather than 6. They are oriented at 75 degrees but spaced about 185 n. miles apart, instead of 8 n. miles

By experiment I have found that if the angle of the design, in a new project, is set before a total effort allocation is entered it is possible to generate multiple suitable designs. Any attempt to change the angle results in the 0 angle number of 6 samplers being inserted and it does not appear to be possible to update this again. Only a brand new project can seem to do what we want.

I am interested to hear any thoughts or suggestions whether this is operator error or a bug.

Paul

Paul

messages.body_plain:
Good to hear this solved the problem.  For the benefit of others:
Distance can cope well with GIS data in either a projected coordinate
system or geographic coordinate system -- but in the latter case a
projection to go from (lat,long) to (x,y) needs to be specified for
survey design to work.  Often the simplest is to work in a projected
coordinate system but to remove the projection files from the Distance
project data folder, so that Distance works with just the plain (x,y)
and doesn't need to deal with projection calculations at all.  This is
covered in Chapter 5 of the help, under Geographic (GIS) data.

Regarding sidescan sonar, I'm not aware of anything, but it's far from
my area of expertise so other listfolk may be.  There was a paper on
estimating krill density from multibeam sonar using distance sampling
ideas (Cox et al. 2011) but I think that's a different topic.

Cheers, Len

Cox, M. et al. 2011. Estimating the density of Antarctic krill
(Euphausia superba) from multi-beam echo-sounder observations using
distance sampling methods. Applied Statistics DOI 10.2307/41057576
Copy at
https://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/~perg/Cox_et_al_J_Roy_Stat_Soc_C_60_2011.pdf
and probably other places.

messages.body_plain:
I am relatively new to DISTANCE and have an analysis question.

I didn’t find relevant discussion in the Dist 7.1 User’s Guide, or in the threads here.

I’ve been given Distance pop estimates (with variance) in each of 4 (2x2) factorial treatments repeated in a number of years. In most cases, I have two estimates for each treatment, each from observations sorted into distance bins (without the possibility of re- or sub-sampling). To find/test for treatment and temporal effects, my instinct is to do a repeated measures ANOVA (or GLM) or its equivalent.

Can someone point me to a relevant resource? Online or published examples? Advise me how to proceed?
